records.concept_details:
Description: Liberalism, from liber meaning free, joined early nationalism to a programme of individual freedom, equality before law, government by consent, constitutional parliamentary representation, an end to autocracy and clerical privilege, and secure private property. Its citizenship was initially restricted: revolutionary France gave voting and election rights exclusively to property-owning men; the Jacobin period briefly widened male suffrage, while the Napoleonic Code restored limits and subordinated women to fathers or husbands. Women and non-propertied men therefore organised through the nineteenth century for equal political rights.
Achieving Mastery: The learner can distinguish legal equality from the restricted political citizenship of nineteenth-century liberalism.

Description: The Treaty of Vienna of 1815 restored the Bourbon dynasty, removed French annexations and reorganised territory to prevent renewed French expansion. records.concept_details:
Description: Repression after 1815 pushed liberal-nationalists into secret societies that trained revolutionaries and opposed restored monarchies. Giuseppe Mazzini, born in Genoa in 1805, joined the Carbonari and was exiled in 1831 after attempting a revolution in Liguria. He founded Young Italy in Marseilles and Young Europe in Berne, seeking a united Italian democratic republic within an alliance of nations because he saw nations as natural units of humanity. Italy’s patchwork of states therefore had to be replaced. His model inspired societies in Germany, France, Switzerland, and Poland and alarmed Metternich.
Achieving Mastery: The learner can connect Mazzini’s secret societies to his goal of a united democratic republic.

records.concept_details:
Description: Johann Gottfried Herder (1744–1803) located authentic German culture in das volk, the common people, whose folk songs, poetry, and dances expressed the volksgeist, or national spirit. Collecting these traditions helped build identity and reach largely illiterate audiences. Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, born in Hanau in 1785 and 1786, gathered tales for six years, published their first collection in 1812, and compiled a 33-volume German dictionary. Their work also resisted French domination.
Achieving Mastery: The learner can use Herder’s volksgeist and Grimm scholarship to explain German cultural nation-building.

records.concept_details:
Description: After Poland was partitioned at the end of the eighteenth century by Russia, Prussia, and Austria, it lacked an independent territory but retained national feeling through music and language. Karol Kurpinski’s operas and music made the polonaise and mazurka nationalist symbols. After the 1831 rebellion against Russian rule was crushed, Russian replaced Polish in schools. Polish clergy used Polish in worship and religious instruction, often suffering imprisonment or exile to Siberia.
Achieving Mastery: The learner can show how language, music, and religion preserved Polish identity under partition.

records.concept_details:
Description: The 1830s brought hardship as population growth produced more job seekers than employment, pushing rural migrants into overcrowded urban slums. records.concept_details:
Description: On 18 May 1848, 831 elected representatives assembled in Frankfurt’s Church of St Paul to draft a constitution for a united German nation whose monarch would answer to a parliament. They offered this crown to Friedrich Wilhelm IV, King of Prussia, but he rejected it and joined aristocratic and military opposition. Middle-class deputies’ resistance to workers and artisans weakened popular support, allowing troops to dissolve the assembly.

Description: In the mid-nineteenth century, political fragmentation prevented a single Italian nation-state: the peninsula and related territories were divided into seven states within dynastic arrangements and the multinational Habsburg Empire. Sardinia-Piedmont alone was ruled by an Italian princely house; Austrian Habsburgs controlled the north, the Pope the centre, and Bourbon kings of Spain the south. records.concept_details:
Description: Britain’s nation-state formed gradually, not through a single revolution or sudden upheaval. Before the eighteenth century there was no British nation; English, Welsh, Scottish, and Irish communities had distinct ethnic, cultural, and political traditions. As England grew wealthier and more powerful, the English Parliament, having taken power from the monarchy in 1688, extended English influence. The Act of Union with Scotland in 1707 created the United Kingdom of Great Britain, with English members dominant.
Achieving Mastery: The learner can explain how English political power and the 1707 union shaped Britain.

records.concept_details:
Description: Germania personified the German nation. Philip Veit’s 1848 banner, prepared for St Paul’s Church during the Frankfurt Parliament in March 1848, showed broken chains for freedom, an eagle breastplate for imperial strength, oak leaves for heroism, a sword for readiness to fight, and an olive branch for peace. The banned black-red-gold flag signalled liberal nationalism and the rising sun a new era; later, Lorenz Clasen’s 1860 image tied Germania to defending the Rhine.
Achieving Mastery: The learner can interpret Germania’s symbols in relation to freedom, strength, peace, and German nationalism.
records.concept_title: Germania and the Symbolic Language of German Nationalism

records.concept_details:
Description: The Balkans included Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia, and Montenegro, whose peoples were broadly identified as Slavs. Much of the region remained under Ottoman rule, but nineteenth-century reforms failed to restore the empire. Romantic nationalism and Ottoman decline encouraged subject nationalities to demand independence or political rights, using memories of earlier freedom and later foreign subjugation to justify their struggles.
Achieving Mastery: The learner can connect Ottoman decline, historical memory, and romantic nationalism to Balkan demands.
records.concept_title: Romantic Nationalism and the Breakup of Ottoman Control in the Balkans
records.keywords: Balkans, Slavs, Ottoman Empire, romantic nationalism, independence, political rights, historical memory, nationalities
records.source_evidence: The most serious source of nationalist tension in Europe after 1871 was the Balkans; subject nationalities broke away from Ottoman control

records.concept_details:
Description: Balkan nationalities competed to define their identities, secure independence, and gain territory from neighbouring states. These local rivalries became more dangerous because Russia, Germany, England, and Austria-Hungary competed for influence, trade, colonies, naval strength, and military advantage. Each sought to weaken rival control and extend its own power in the Balkans. The resulting series of regional wars helped create the conditions that led to the First World War in 1914.
Achieving Mastery: The learner can trace how local Balkan rivalries became more dangerous through great-power competition.

records.concept_details:
Description: A map celebrating the British Empire links national pride with colonial domination. Britannia, the symbol of the British nation, sits triumphantly over the globe; angels carry a banner of freedom; and colonies are represented through tigers, elephants, forests and images labelled as primitive people. The celebratory composition presents worldwide domination as the basis of Britain’s national pride.

records.concept_details:
Description: During and after nineteenth-century European colonial expansion, colonised peoples formed anti-imperial movements to end foreign domination and create independent nation-states. Their nationalism grew through collective unity forged in opposition to imperial rule, but it did not simply reproduce European models; each society developed its own form. At the same time, organising political life through nation-states increasingly came to be regarded as a natural and universal principle.
Achieving Mastery: The learner can explain how resistance to colonial rule produced distinctive movements for nation-state independence.
records.concept_title: Colonised Peoples’ Nationalist Struggle for Independent Nation-states
records.keywords: anti-imperial movements, colonised peoples, independent nation-states, collective unity, national identity, universal nation-state
records.source_evidence: Colonised countries began to oppose imperial domination; people everywhere developed their own specific variety of nationalism
